title: The Future is Bright: NICA Expands with Its First Western Regional Event in St. George, Utah
content:
Last weekend, NICA (the National Interscholastic Cycling Association) hosted its first-ever Western Regional event in St. George, Utah. I was fortunate to be invited by NICA’s first non-endemic partner, Mazda, to take a road trip and attend the event in person. This allowed me to observe the NICA experience firsthand and see the level of participation, community, inclusivity, and love of cycling being fostered by the world’s largest youth mountain biking organization. 

Of course, I also got to see some of the top youth mountain bike racers from across NICA’s western leagues battle it out on course in the biggest race of the season. Let me tell ya, these kids are quick.

NICA Regional Events

Since it was founded in 2009, NICA has been growing steadily and has become the largest youth mountain bike racing association in the U.S. and the world. In its 17-year history, it has expanded across the U.S. (and recently to Australia) and has grown to 33 leagues nationwide, including over 1,000 teams, more than 26,000 youth athletes, and 16,000 adult coaches.

In recent years, NICA has expanded to include regional events across the U.S. to bring together and celebrate the NICA community with weekend-long festivals that include rides, races, expos, and other activities. The racing is open to male and female high-school-aged (grades 9-12) athletes in a tiered varsity system: JV3, JV2, JV1, and Varsity. The events also include several non-competitive activities, including adventure rides, GRiT, skill areas, and Teen Trail Corps (more on these below).

These events started with Eastern Regionals in 2023 and 2024, with NICA adding Central Regionals in 2025. In early 2026, NICA announced the addition of Western Regionals to its calendar, providing an opportunity for all of its leagues to participate in a Regional event. This week, NICA announced its 2027 Regional event schedule, which will include all three regions for the second year in a row. Additionally, as part of a new multi-year partnership, NICA’s 2027 Regional events are being presented by Mazda (more on this soon).

Inaugural Western Regionals

Taking place in St. George, Utah, this past weekend, the first Western Regionals drew participants from 10 western leagues representing the states of Arizona, California, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, and Utah. This included over 800 high-school-aged racers, more than 120 youth participants in non-competitive activities, and nearly 600 volunteer adult coaches.

Including families and spectators, well over 2,000 attendees came to the race venue in St. George to participate or support. They were greeted by 22 vendors in the expo area, including NICA’s lead partners like Trek, Mazda, RockShox, and SRAM, along with neutral support from Shimano and Canyon, and pit areas for all of the NICA leagues in attendance. Mountain bike races were nothing like this when I was a kid…

Beyond the expo and the sheer number of athletes, coaches, and spectators, I was immediately struck by the scale of the production, particularly the organization and professional setup of the venue. NICA, it seems, runs a very tight ship, and this was legitimately one of the best-organized events that I’ve seen in years. 

Purpose-Built Race Venue

As I was walking around and checking out the race course and venue, known as Renegade Ridge Trail Park, it struck me that it seemed oddly ideal for hosting mountain bike races. Not only was there ample parking and a large expo area, but the trail layout included a wide start area, feed zone, and a separate finish area. The trails were freshly cut and in pristine condition, and included rock-armored technical up and downhill sections. Frankly, it reminded me of a World Cup XC course.

After chatting with a few folks, I quickly learned that Renegade Ridge Trail Park was only completed a few months prior, in July, and was purpose-built to NICA race standards to host race events. Through a cooperative effort between Desert Color (resort), Washington County, and the Utah Trust Lands Administration, this new park was built to serve as both a competition venue and public trail network.  

Renegade Ridge Trail Park was first used for the Utah NICA State Championships in late October. With more than 7,000 student-athletes, Utah is NICA’s largest league, and its State Championships reportedly drew 2,400+ participants. Say what?

The Racing

NICA’s roots are in racing, and it is one of its core activities. According to NICA, their “inclusive racing format offers participants the opportunity to experience and learn discipline, success, failure, and graceful defeat,” while the “team environment helps student-athletes learn empathy, humility, flexibility, and resilience.” And as I observed over the weekend, it truly takes a village. Sure, bike racing is an individual sport, but these young athletes are supported by their coaches, teammates, friends, and family.

With over 800 racers competing across four categories (each with separate male and female races), there were a total of 8 races over the weekend. The four-tier varsity system — JV3, JV2, JV1, and Varsity — offers racing for athletes of varying experience and fitness levels, from entry-level up to those who might go pro in the coming years. 

On that note, NICA has become somewhat of a hotbed of up-and-coming athletes and a feeder system of sorts for top-level U.S. mountain biking. It has absolutely been instrumental in helping elevate the level of mountain bike racing in the U.S. and on the world stage. In fact, Brendan Quirk, the CEO of USA Cycling, was in attendance at NICA Western Regionals. He spoke briefly during a Q&A at the event, saying, “Our mountain bike program is as strong as it has ever been, and that is a direct result of NICA.” He pointed out that 100% of the top U.S. mountain bike racers are NICA alumni, and went on to say, “If you have aspirations to race professionally, this is where you want to be.” 

Familiar names including Kate Courtney, Gwendalyn Gibson, Savilia Blunk, Haley Batten, Madigan Munro, Christopher Blevins, Bjorn Riley, and Riley Amos all came up through NICA before making their way onto the world stage. Not to mention NICA alumni like Sepp Kuss and Neilson Powless, who went on to professional road racing careers. 

And it’s clear to see why. The level of racing is already incredibly high. On Sunday, the pace of the Varsity Male and Female races was very impressive. In the Varsity Female race, the top five were separated by just 15 seconds. Similarly, in the Varsity Male race, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th places were decided in an exciting 3-up sprint just 2 seconds behind the race winner — the top 15 all finished within 2 minutes of the leader. 

Of course, any of these racers and their fellow competitors could potentially go on to become professional racers. And with 26,000 NICA athletes and growing across the country, it certainly seems like U.S. mountain biking’s upward trajectory is bound to continue.

More Than Just Racing

NICA’s roots are in racing, and mountain bike racing is obviously still a major part of what the organization does. While those who wish to compete have ample opportunity, NICA’s mission and programs extend well beyond racing. Through its teams, trained coaches, and events, NICA aims to “help young people thrive both on and off the bike — building confidence, leadership, friendships, and making the world a better place.”

  • Our Mission: We build strong minds, bodies, character, and communities through cycling. 
  • Our Vision: Every youth is empowered to be a part of a thriving and engaged cycling community.
  • Our Values: Fun, inclusivity, equity, respect, and community.

Everyone Participates

While some NICA athletes might be all about the racing, non-competitive activities are a staple of NICA events. One of the non-competitive programs is NICA Adventure, where participants get outdoors, learn skills, and experience mountain biking outside of the race course. At Western Regionals, I watched as dozens, if not hundreds, of student athletes and families rode the adventure course at Renegade Ridge Trail Park. The skills zone was also getting plenty of use with a handful of features, including wooden ramps, rollovers, and a teeter-totter to test your bike skills.

Likewise, NICA’s GRiT (Girls Riding Together) is an effort to close the gender gap by bringing more girls and women into the community. NICA’s female participation is already impressive, but the goal is to increase female athlete and coach participation by 10% in the next 5 years. NICA’s Teen Trail Corps programs provide athletes the opportunity to get involved in their cycling community through advocacy activities, including trail building and maintenance. 

Community Building

At Western Regionals, I heard the word “community” probably close to 100 times, and I wasn’t even there the whole time. While it might have initially sounded a little cliché to a jaded old fart like me, it was abundantly clear that it wasn’t just a word in NICA’s mission statement, but it is, in fact, a very big part of the experience. There’s a lot more NICA than just showing up for a race. 

Every NICA team has athletes, coaches, and families involved, and they train and travel together, camp out, and support each other. As these teams go to league events or regionals, their communities and connections grow. I was honestly blown away by the number of student-athletes in attendance, but even more impressed by the number of coaches, family, and friends there to support them.  

And that’s what it’s all about. Success on the race course is great and all, but ultimately, it’s the campfires, dinners, friendships, and camaraderie that will likely leave a lasting impression on all those involved. And that translated directly to sportsmanship and respect on the race course. At the finish line, there was no shortage of high-fives and hugs between athletes, which is always great to see in such a competitive environment. 

My Takeaway

When I first arrived at NICA Western Regionals, I wandered into the expo area and ran into my friend Wayne Smith (aka Big Tall Wayne), a professional race mechanic for Canyon Bicycles, who was on hand providing neutral service for athletes. The weekend had only just started, and he said, “This is easily my favorite event of the year.” And this was coming from a man who has spent the past several years traveling to major professional races around the globe as Pete Stetina’s bike mechanic. 

And I think Big Tall Wayne’s sentiment was shared by many in attendance at Western Regionals. Everything from the venue, participation, organization, and even the weather was spot on. The racing was fast, and the vibes were high. And if there’s one thing I’m taking away, it’s that mountain biking is alive, well, and thriving, and the future of the sport, both on and off the race course, is as bright as it’s ever been. Keep up the good work, NICA.

To learn more about NICA or get involved, head to nationalmtb.org
author: Jeremy Benson
